--- title: "Identifying Priority EEZ Regions for Oyster and Lingcod Aquaculture Using SST and Bathymetric Data" description: "Using environmental suitability modeling to identify the best Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZs) for developing marine aquaculture." image: longcog.jpg date: "12/12/2025" categories: [R, Geospatial Analysis, Aquaculture] draft: false format: html: embed-resources: true standalone: true toc: true code-fold: true editor: markdown: wrap: 72 editor_options: chunk_output_type: console --- ## Purpose ![**Image: Commercial Fishing Boats, Santa Barbara Harbor, California, USA.**](Harbor.png) Global seafood demand is projected to increase by 70% by 2050, yet wild capture fisheries have plateaued near their maximum sustainable yield (Gentry et al., 2017). Marine aquaculture has emerged as a critical pathway to meet this demand, offering a more sustainable protein source than land-based meat production (Hall et al., 2011). Along the U.S. West Coast, this opportunity is particularly significant, the region supports some of the most productive marine ecosystems in the world, driven by seasonal upwelling along the California Current System. However, identifying *where* aquaculture should occur is not straightforward. Optimal sites must balance ecological suitability, species-specific environmental tolerances, and jurisdictional boundaries. Poorly sited operations risk low yields, ecosystem disruption, and regulatory conflict. Geospatial suitability modeling offers a systematic, reproducible framework for narrowing down priority zones before costly on-the-ground assessments are made. ### Research Question: What Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZ) on the U.S. West Coast of the are best suited to developing marine aquaculture for several species of oysters and Lingcod *Ophiodon elongatus* (Girard, 1854)? ### Data Sources I combined three geospatial datasets: - **Bathymetry:** GEBCO 2022 global depth raster\ - **Sea Surface Temperature (SST):** 2008–2012 annual averages\ - **Exclusive Economic Zones:** Cleaned U.S. West Coast EEZ shapefile Species-specific environmental requirements were sourced from FishBase (2025)for Lingcod and SeaLifeBase (2025) for oyster, along with peer-reviewed fisheries literature. All geospatial processing was performed in **R** using `terra`, `stars`, and `sf`. ## Methods Key geospatial techniques included combining vector and raster data, resampling rasters to a common resolution, masking by jurisdictional boundaries, and applying map algebra to identify jointly suitable habitat. #### 1. Prepare SST and Depth Data Certain packages were required prior to the analysis. I loaded in the necessary libraries to proceed with data importation. Then, I read in the depth and EEZ shapefiles using `read_stars` and `st_read`, respectively, Finally, I stacked five annual SST rasters (2008–2012) using `rast()`. It was also important to cross reference each spatial object so that each coordinate reference system (CRS) matches to prevent misalignment (refer to repository linked above for additional information). Here, I calculated the mean SST using `app()` across all year rasters, then converted temperatures from Kelvin to Celsius. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Calculate the SST average mean_sst <- app(sst[[c("average_annual_sst_2008", "average_annual_sst_2009", "average_annual_sst_2010", "average_annual_sst_2011", "average_annual_sst_2012")]], fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE) # Convert average SST from Kelvin to Celsius sst_mean_celsius <- mean_sst - 273.15 ``` ::: Then, I cropped the bathymetry layer to the average SST raster and resampled to match the SST resolution. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # First convert depth stars to SpatRaster depth_rast <- rast(depth) depth_resample <- depth_rast %>% crop(sst_mean_celsius) %>% # crop depth to match SST extent # Resample to match SST resolution, use method near resample(sst_mean_celsius, method = "near") ``` ::: ## Identify Suitable Habitat for Oysters According to the literature, the following conditions are required for optimal growth in oyster species: - **Sea Surface Temperature (SST) Range:** 11–30°C - **Depth Range:** 0–70 m Here, I classified suitable ranges for oyster-specific depth and SST by applying an if-else statement to categorize values based on a conditional. I assigned a value of 0 for values that fell outside the required range and assigned a value of 1 for values that were within the range. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Reclassify SST (11-30°C suitable for oysters) sst_suitable <- app(sst_mean_celsius, fun = function(x){ ifelse(x >= 11 & x <= 30,1,0) # if temperate is between 11- 30 °C, return 1, else 0 }) # Reclassify Suitable depth range (0-70 meters for oysters) depth_suitable <- app(depth_resample, fun = function(x){ ifelse(x >= -70 & x <= 0,1,0) # select depths from 0 to 70 meters below surface. }) # Multiply the two suitability raster suitable_locations <- sst_suitable * depth_suitable ``` ::: ## Quantify Suitable Area Within Each EEZ I rasterized EEZ polygons, masked suitability values, and computed cell-area using zonal statistics. Here, I rasterized the EEZ shapefile based on suitable locations for each region (rgn). Then, I created a mask to isolate suitable locations within EEZs and summed the suitable area of each EEZ region. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Rasterize the EEZ data (creates zone IDs) eez_raster <- rasterize(eez, suitable_locations, field = "rgn") #Calculate cell area with cellSize() cell_area <- cellSize(suitable_locations, unit = "km") # Mask suitable locations to EEZ boundaries suitable_area <- mask(suitable_locations, eez) * cell_area # Sum suitable are by EEZ zonal statistics eez_suitable <- zonal(suitable_area, eez_raster, fun = "sum", na.rm = TRUE) ``` ::: ## Results **Oyster Suitability** The highest-ranked region was Central California with about 4,940 km² of suitable area (\~34% of all suitable habitat). The lowest ranked region was Northern California with about 454.30 km² (3.1% of all suitable area). ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
EEZ Rankings by Suitable Aquaculture Area
Rank EEZ Region Suitable Area (km²) % of Total
1 Central California 4940.04 34.1
2 Southern California 4221.39 29.1
3 Washington 3313.16 22.8
4 Oregon 1578.97 10.9
5 Northern California 454.30 3.1
````` ::: ::: **Map 1.** Oyster Aquaculture Suitability by EEZ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Map with tmap basic # Map with tmap basic tm_basemap("CartoDB.Positron", alpha = 0.7) + tm_shape(eez_ranked) + tm_polygons("suitable_area_km2", palette = "-mako", style = "cont", title = "Suitable Area (km²)", border.col = "black", border.lwd = 0.5) + tm_layout(main.title = "Suitable Oyster Aquaculuture Area by EEZ", main.title.size = 1.2, legend.outside = TRUE, frame = FALSE) + tm_text("rgn", # Label by region size = .8, # Adjust size col = "white", # Adjust text color fontface = "bold", # Labels are bolded xmod = -.5) + # Adjust .5 from the left tm_compass(type = "4star", position = c("right", "top")) + tm_scalebar(position = c("left", "bottom")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Suitable oyster aquaculture area by U.S. West Coast EEZ, based on mean SST (2008–2012) and bathymetric depth. Central California (CA-C) ranked highest with 4,940 km².](aqua_blog_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: # Repeat previous steps with species of choice by creating a Function ![**Image: Lingcod (*Ophiodon elongatus*), California Coast.**](longcog.jpg) Lingcod (*Ophiodon elongatus*) is one of the most commercially and recreationally important groundfish on the U.S. West Coast, prized for its firm white flesh, it's the fish behind the classic Pacific fish and chips. Native from Alaska to Baja California, Lingcod are demersal predators that occupy rocky reef habitats at depths typically between 10–100 m and prefer cool temperate waters. **Lingcod Suitable Conditions (FishBase, 2026):** - **Sea Surface Temperature Range:** 7–18°C - **Depth Range:** 0–100 m The suitability workflow is generalizable to any species with documented SST and depth tolerances. Below, the same function is applied to Lingcod using its species-specific environmental ranges. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # The function takes the following arguments: # sst raster file # depth raster file # minimum and maximum sea surface temperature # minimum and maximum depth # species name find_suitable_aquaculture <- function(sst_raster, depth_raster, eez_sf, sst_min, sst_max, depth_min, depth_max, species_name) { # Reclassify SST sst_suitable <- app(sst_raster, fun = function(x) { ifelse(x >= sst_min & x <= sst_max, 1, 0) }) # Reclassify depth depth_suitable <- app(depth_raster, fun = function(x) { ifelse(x >= depth_min & x <= depth_max, 1, 0) }) # Find suitable locations (both conditions) suitable_locations <- sst_suitable * depth_suitable names(suitable_locations) <- species_name # Mask to EEZ suitable_in_eez <- mask(suitable_locations, eez_sf) # Rasterize EEZ eez_rasterize <- rasterize(eez_sf, suitable_locations, field = "rgn") # Calculate cell areas cell_area_km2 <- cellSize(suitable_locations, unit = "km") # Calculate suitable area per cell (commented out for now) suitable_area <- suitable_in_eez * cell_area_km2 # Sum by EEZ zone eez_suitable_area <- zonal( suitable_area, eez_rasterize, fun = "sum", na.rm = TRUE) colnames(eez_suitable_area) <- c("EEZ_ID", "Suitable_Area_km2") # Join with EEZ data and rank eez_sf$suitable_area_km2 <- eez_suitable_area$Suitable_Area_km2[ match(eez_sf$rgn, eez_suitable_area$EEZ_ID)] eez_ranked <- eez_sf[order(-eez_sf$suitable_area_km2), ] # Create summary table summary_table <- data.frame( Rank = 1:nrow(eez_ranked), EEZ = eez_ranked$rgn, Suitable_Area_km2 = round(eez_ranked$suitable_area_km2, 2) ) # Return results as a list results <- list( species = species_name, sst_suitable = sst_suitable, depth_suitable = depth_suitable, suitable_locations = suitable_locations, suitable_in_eez = suitable_in_eez, eez_ranked = eez_ranked, summary_table = summary_table ) return(results) } ``` ::: ## Lingcod Suitability Results Here I apply `find_suitable_aquaculture()` to Lingcod using its cold-water, shallow demersal habitat requirements. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Lingcod suitable habitat lingcod_results <- find_suitable_aquaculture( sst_raster = sst_mean_celsius, depth_raster = depth_resample, eez_sf = eez, sst_min = 7, sst_max = 18, depth_min = -100, depth_max = 0, species_name = "Lingcod" ) # Access results kable(lingcod_results$summary_table) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | Rank|EEZ | Suitable_Area_km2| |----:|:-------------------|-----------------:| | 1|Washington | 10569.13| | 2|Oregon | 8317.53| | 3|Central California | 7775.55| | 4|Southern California | 6092.77| | 5|Northern California | 5212.83| ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Plot Crab EEZ tm_basemap("CartoDB.Positron", alpha = 0.7) + tm_shape(lingcod_results$eez_ranked) + tm_polygons("suitable_area_km2", palette = "-mako", style = "cont", title = "Suitable Area (km²)", border.col = "black", border.lwd = 0.5) + tm_layout(main.title = "Suitable Lingcod Aquaculture Area by EEZ", main.title.size = 1.2, legend.outside = TRUE, frame = FALSE) + tm_text("rgn", # Label by region size = .8, # Adjust size col = "white", # Adjust text color fontface = "bold", # Labels are bolded xmod = -.5) + # Adjust .5 from the left tm_compass(type = "4star", position = c("right", "top")) + tm_scale_bar(position = c("left", "bottom")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Suitable Lingcod aquaculture area by U.S. West Coast EEZ based on mean SST (2008–2012, 7–18°C) and depth (0–100 m). Washington ranked highest with 10,569 km².](aqua_blog_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Discussion Among the West Coast EEZs, **Central California ranked highest for oyster cultivation** with 4,940 km² of suitable area, reflecting its warmer nearshore SSTs and broad shallow shelf. **Northern California ranked lowest** at 454 km², where strong coastal upwelling keeps temperatures near the lower bound of oyster tolerance. Lingcod showed a strikingly different spatial pattern. **Washington ranked first** with 10,569 km² of suitable habitat, followed by Oregon (8,318 km²) and Central California (7,776 km²). This northward shift reflects Lingcod's cold-water preference, the cooler SSTs that limit oyster suitability in Washington and Oregon fall squarely within Lingcod's optimal thermal range. Together, the two species illustrate how environmental tolerances drive fundamentally different regional priorities for aquaculture development. Several limitations apply. SST and depth alone cannot capture substrate type, Lingcod strongly prefer rocky reef habitat, which this analysis cannot resolve. Marine protected areas, tribal waters, harmful algal bloom frequency, and shipping lane conflicts are also unaccounted for. Future analyses could incorporate substrate classification and multi-criteria decision frameworks to better reflect real-world siting constraints. ### References Lam, L. S., Basnett, B.
